name: Aldous Harding
label: 4AD
lede: Aldous Harding busked her way out of Lyttelton, sings in about six different voices, keeps her lyrics to herself, and has made three of her five albums at the same Welsh studio with the same producer.

eras.title: From a flaxseed farm to the streets of Lyttelton
eras.text: Hannah Topp grows up between Dunedin and a flaxseed farm in Geraldine, sings on her mother's record at 13, and busks her way into the Lyttelton scene near Christchurch. Her debut gets made in a makeshift studio while the city is still shaking.

years.h: Hannah Sian Topp is born, and later takes a stepfather's surname
years.p: Her mother is the Canadian-born folk singer [[Lorina Harding|1053f346-3f4b-4277-a18a-9ffab48b66ef]]. 'Aldous' came from wanting a name that sounded like a manly Alice, according to Wikipedia.
years.xp:
Wikipedia gives her birthplace as Lyttelton. AudioCulture and a 2014 interview have her born in Auckland and raised in Dunedin until she was 11, then on an organic flaxseed farm outside Geraldine. The farm hosted an annual folk festival, and she headlined the last one in 2016.

Harding is her stepfather's surname. She describes herself as a fearful, lonely kid who danced in her pyjamas to the radio.

years.h: Thirteen, and singing on her mother's record
years.p: Lorina Harding's album Clean Break won a Tui for best folk album. Wikipedia lists her daughter's song as 'Exactly What to Say'.
years.xp: AudioCulture says she resisted a music career for years, because she tied it to being poor, separated and never home. She finished school at Logan Park High School in Dunedin, singing with friends [[Nadia Reid|2485f75b-bbac-4c9d-8bf2-da323bd7ccfa]] and Flora Knight, and wrote her first songs as poems she couldn't accompany.

years.h: Adam McGrath hears a busker, and has her onstage by evening
years.p: McGrath of [[The Eastern|69b718c9-4979-4bd7-9ca0-e9b3a8e6644c]] had her sing with the band that night at the Wunderbar in Lyttelton.
years.xp: McGrath remembered that she 'made everyone lose their breath with her voice and attitude and of course her bravery.' After travelling in Europe and Quebec she rejoined the band a year later and played with them for a couple of years, opening for Old Crow Medicine Show and Fleetwood Mac, according to NZ Musician.

years.big: Where creative types go to die
q: Where creative types go to die
years.h: Lyttelton is home, and she's blunt about it
years.p: Harding on the port town's other side: 'a lot of drugs and alcohol.' She moved there at the end of 2008 and still calls it the place she feels most at home.
years.xp: Wikipedia quotes her on the harbour town near Christchurch: it is 'sort of where sometimes it feels like that's where creative types go to die.' Through The Eastern she met the producer Ben Edwards and the singer [[Marlon Williams|92677e54-c738-4e33-8c08-e51ba490285b]].

years.h: The Christchurch earthquake hits while she's busking in Cashel Mall
years.p: She was unhurt and went home to Geraldine. That October a bakery busk got her an opening slot for Anika Moa, who lent her a week of recording space in Auckland.
years.xp: Those Auckland recordings were never released, according to AudioCulture. The debut she had started with Edwards and Williams was interrupted by the February quake and picked up again the following year.

years.h: A concrete room under a supermarket, and a debut cut in pieces
years.p: Harding records with Ben Edwards and [[Marlon Williams|92677e54-c738-4e33-8c08-e51ba490285b]] in a makeshift Lyttelton studio. Part of it was cut under the Wunderbar, which had no toilet.
years.xp:
AudioCulture puts the sessions in a concrete studio beneath the Lyttelton supermarket. In a 2014 interview she says part of the record was made under the Wunderbar and part at Edwards's studio, and that Edwards was an old friend.

She described the finished record as a story of a battle between good and evil that's in everybody. The oldest song, 'Hunter', was about four years old by then.

eras.title: Out of Lyttelton, into Bristol
eras.text: The debut comes out on Lyttelton Records with Flying Nun behind it. Harding follows Marlon Williams to Melbourne, where a friend connects her with the producer who will shape everything after.

years.h: Aldous Harding comes out on Lyttelton Records and Flying Nun
years.p: Nine songs of gothic folk. It reached number 35 in New Zealand, per Wikipedia.
years.xp:
Critic Nick Bollinger, quoted by AudioCulture, said her voice 'shifted the air with rarefied grace.' Her live sets around then included a cover of Toto's 'Africa', she told Witchdoctor.

She later said she had no idea how that sound came out of her on the early songs.

years.cap: Aldous Harding and Marlon Williams share a mic, November 2015
years.h: Melbourne, and a tip from Laura Jean
years.p: Harding moves to Melbourne after Marlon Williams. The musician [[Laura Jean|4bb7a54a-00a6-46eb-b054-df54895695ee]] puts her in touch with [[John Parish|4ae92e70-3690-473b-8fbc-49749565669f]], the man behind [[PJ Harvey|e795e03d-b5d5-4a5f-834d-162cfb308a2c]]'s records.
years.xp: AudioCulture reports that Laura Jean made the connection. Parish, born in 1959, co-founded Automatic Dlamini in 1982; PJ Harvey played in it from 1988 to 1991, and the two made Dance Hall at Louse Point in 1996.

years.cap: Harding on acoustic guitar, London, November 2016
years.h: Bristol, and a studio called J & J
years.p: Harding flies to England to record Party with Parish at J & J Studio. [[Fenne Lily|cd295735-b68a-4b5d-aa10-de0dea37ca89]] and Mike Hadreas of [[Perfume Genius|c4ff10e0-ae5a-467d-a409-6e0b4bf241eb]] guest.
years.xp: Harding called Parish gentle and patient, but said the two 'rub up against each other like two old porcupines.' The working relationship ran on through Party, Designer, Warm Chris and Train on the Island.

eras.title: Party and the 4AD deal
eras.text: 4AD signs her and releases Party worldwide alongside Flying Nun. The videos get stranger, the voice keeps changing character, and the awards start arriving.

years.cap: Harding in a white suit at Omeara, London, May 22, 2017
years.src: Wikipedia: Party (Aldous Harding album) · Wikipedia: Aldous Harding · AudioCulture
years.h: Party is her first 4AD album
years.p: Parish produced it. 'Horizon' came out as the first single on 10 February.
years.xp:
Party charted at number 6 in New Zealand and won the 2017 NZ Music Awards for Breakthrough Artist and Alternative. Metacritic gives it 83 from 11 reviews. The Guardian called her 'one of the most original songwriters around', and Jon Pareles of The New York Times said her exposed voice 'changes character from song to song'.

She played 'Horizon' on BBC Two's Later... with Jools Holland the same evening as [[Lorde|8e494408-8620-4c6a-82c2-c2ca4a1e4f12]], and AudioCulture says the studio lights magnified her facial quirks.

years.h: Mike Hadreas sings on 'Imagining My Man'
years.p: Hadreas, who records as Perfume Genius, joins the second single from Party. Charlotte Evans directed the video.

years.cap: Harding at the Fairgrounds Festival, December 9, 2017
years.src: Wikipedia: Aldous Harding · AudioCulture · Wikipedia: Party (Aldous Harding album)
years.h: Party wins the Taite Prize
years.p: New Zealand's album of the year prize, for a record made in Bristol by a Lyttelton busker.
years.xp: AudioCulture adds that 'Horizon' was runner-up for the APRA Silver Scroll, narrowly losing to Lorde. The 'Blend' video, in a cowgirl look AudioCulture compares to Apocalypse Now, arrived on 12 June 2017.

eras.title: Designer and the Silver Scroll
eras.text: She trades the sad-girl frame for shuffling beats and a Welsh backing band, then writes a song that wins New Zealand's top songwriting prize.

years.h: Designer is cut at Rockfield with H. Hawkline on bass
years.p: Recorded in Wales with Parish. Hawkline also plays guitar and keyboards.
years.xp:
AudioCulture says she recruited musicians from [[Cate Le Bon|f2393e49-b791-46da-a6d7-1e9e60743405]]'s band, Hawkline (Huw Evans) among them, and brought a levity and playfulness that hadn't been there before. Pitchfork gave it 8.0 and Metacritic averages 88; it reached number 5 in New Zealand.

Wikipedia lists the extras: saxophone from Stephen Black and violin from Clare Mactaggart.

years.cap: Harding with her band at EartH, London, May 22, 2019
years.h: 'The Barrel' takes the 2019 APRA Silver Scroll
years.p: New Zealand's songwriting award goes to a song whose meaning she won't explain.
years.xp: Designer won the Alternative category at the 2019 NZ Music Awards and was a finalist for the 2020 Taite Music Prize. Harding has said she tries not to explain her songs: 'I know exactly what my songs are about, and I try not to tell people.'

eras.title: A Cardiff move and a first number one
eras.text: She writes at her mother's house in lockdown, settles in Cardiff near H. Hawkline, and cuts Warm Chris at Rockfield. It becomes her first number one at home.

years.h: Lockdown at her mother's house, then Cardiff
years.p: She writes the Warm Chris songs in Geraldine, then settles in the Welsh capital where Hawkline lives.
years.xp: RNZ says much of the record was written during 2020's lockdown at her mother's home in Geraldine before she went to Wales to record. AudioCulture has her settling in Cardiff that year.

years.h: Warm Chris gives her a first number one at home
years.p: Made at Rockfield Studios in Monmouthshire with Parish and Hawkline.
years.xp: Pitchfork's Sophie Kemp praised 'some of Harding's best songwriting yet', and AudioCulture reports the score as 8.2. Metacritic averages 82, and Clash gave it 9/10. 'Tick Tock' reached number 31 on the New Zealand singles chart and 'Ennui' 40.

years.big: I really do feel more like an actor.
q: I really do feel more like an actor.
years.h: Musician fits her less and less, she tells RNZ
years.p: Harding says so in an interview around Warm Chris.
years.xp: 'A musician is something that I resonate with less and less,' she told RNZ. She also said listeners don't need to know what she was thinking and that explaining could be detrimental. Her clips, including the ones with director Martin Sagadin, lean on the acting.

years.cap: Harding on the Warm Chris tour, October 22, 2022
years.h: Jason Williamson of Sleaford Mods guests on 'Leathery Whip'
years.p: The Nottingham frontman [[Jason Williamson|efb4c486-56b3-4b1f-a7e8-0cd4e65a9ee7]] appears on the closing track of Warm Chris.
years.xp: RNZ has Harding saying she was drawn to the [[Sleaford Mods|09d8290b-6ada-422f-8ce3-19349fb1c15d]] frontman's physicality and power. Wikipedia credits Williamson as a guest vocalist.

years.cap: H. Hawkline in Harding's band, Barbican, London, April 28, 2023
years.h: Hawkline opens at Tramshed in Cardiff, then plays in her band
years.p: Huw Evans warms up alone with an electric guitar and a tape machine. Harding's set includes 'Fever' and 'The Barrel'.
years.xp: Buzz's review of the night says Hawkline's 26-minute solo set drew on his 2023 album Milk for Flowers and 'rawness in his voice'. Harding's band, with him in it, followed her 'shapeshifting voice'.

eras.title: Train on the Island
eras.text: Four years after Warm Chris, Harding returns with her fifth record, again made with Parish at Rockfield, and Pitchfork calls it her best.

years.src: Rolling Stone Australia · Brighton and Hove News
years.h: 'One Stop' leads off the fifth album
years.p: Michelle Henning directed the video. The song premiered on BBC 6 Music's Huw Stephens show.
years.xp: The announcement came with her first headline shows since 2023, and a limited run of just 50 copies on 'Holiday Records Copper' vinyl, per Rolling Stone Australia.

years.src: Stereogum: Aldous Harding & H. Hawkline · Paste · God Is In The TV
years.h: H. Hawkline joins her for 'Venus in the Zinnia'
years.p: The video mixes FaceTime footage of the two with Harding floating over the earth.
years.xp: Stereogum credits the video to Harding, Martin Sagadin, Hopey Parish and Michelle Henning, and notes John Parish's Wurlitzer. God Is In The TV and Stereogum both call it a duet with Hawkline; Paste has Parish as the partner.

years.src: Wikipedia: Train on the Island · Paste · Stereogum: Aldous Harding Announces
years.h: Train on the Island arrives to a Best New Music tag
years.p: Pitchfork gives it 9.0, and Jayson Greene calls it her career-best album.
years.xp:
Ten songs in 39 minutes, cut at Rockfield with Parish, Hawkline, drummer Seb Rochford of Polar Bear, harpist Mali Llywelyn, synth player Thomas Poli and pedal steel player Joe Harvey-Whyte. Metacritic averages 87 from 14 reviews, and it reached number 4 in New Zealand.

Paste's Miranda Wollen calls it a 'silly, colorful triumph'. Under the Radar's Mark Moody calls it a mixed bag. 'Coats', the closer, came out as a single two days before the album.

years.src: Brighton and Hove News · Rolling Stone Australia
years.h: The Barbican sells out twice, so a third night goes on
years.p: UK and European dates run May to August with Vera Ellen supporting. North America follows in September and October.
years.xp: Brighton and Hove News lists the Dome on 25 May and the added London show on 31 May.
